scenarios.name: Wildfire Watch
scenarios.objective: Image fire-prone areas every 2 days for 3 years, and get the pictures to firefighters fast.

measurements.name: Heat from active fires
measurements.why: Fires glow brightly in infrared light, even through thin smoke.

measurements.name: Smoke plumes and burned land
measurements.why: Smoke and fresh burn scars show where a fire is and which way it is spreading.

goals.name: Find areas at risk before they burn

measurements.name: Dry plants
measurements.why: Dry plants reflect light differently from healthy green ones, and they burn easily.

scenarios.tooltip: Firefighters need to know about new fires quickly. A small CubeSat can watch for them, if it can get its pictures home in time.
scenarios.sourceNote: A 6U CubeSat mission. Build time from CubeSat 101 (typically 18 to 24 months); budget keeps CubeSat 101's advice of at least a 10% reserve.

scenarios.name: Flood Radar
scenarios.objective: Map flooding during storms, when clouds hide the ground, every 2 days for 3 years.

measurements.name: The ground under storm clouds
measurements.why: Storms bring thick clouds. Radar waves pass straight through them, and work at night too.

measurements.name: Flooded land on clear days
measurements.why: Between storms, water and wet ground look different from dry land in several colours of light.

scenarios.tooltip: When rivers burst during a storm, rescue teams need maps, but clouds block normal cameras. A radar satellite can see through them, if it has enough power.
scenarios.sourceNote: A user-segment-led mission (disaster agencies need maps within hours). Radar sees through clouds and at night. Budget and build time are game estimates sized for a small satellite with a radar.

scenarios.name: Ship Watch
scenarios.objective: Track ships far out at sea every 2 days for 2 years, and spot ones that switch off their tracker.

goals.name: Know where ships are at sea

measurements.name: Ship positions from their radio messages
measurements.why: Big ships broadcast their name, position and speed by AIS radio. From orbit a CubeSat can hear them far beyond the reach of coast stations.

measurements.name: Ships seen from above
measurements.why: A ship that switches off its AIS still shows up in images, so a camera can catch it.

scenarios.tooltip: Coast guards need to know which ships are where, even far out at sea. A small CubeSat can listen for the radio messages every big ship sends.
scenarios.sourceNote: Based on real AIS CubeSats such as AAUSAT-3, which showed a 1U CubeSat with a simple dipole antenna can receive AIS from low Earth orbit. Budget, schedule and revisit are game estimates.

scenarios.name: Storm Tracker
scenarios.objective: Watch one half of the Earth all the time from geostationary orbit for 10 years, so forecasters can follow storms as they grow.

measurements.name: Clouds and moisture, all the time
measurements.why: Pictures of clouds and water vapour every few minutes show where storms form and how fast they move. This is the GOES-R mission's key measurement.

measurements.name: Lightning flashes
measurements.why: A sudden jump in lightning can warn that a storm is getting stronger, before radar or pictures show it.

scenarios.tooltip: A big weather satellite that hovers over one spot and never looks away. It must be light enough for its rocket and fit the budget, and it needs fuel to stay in place for 10 years.
scenarios.sourceNote: NASA GOES-R design overview: continuous imagery of the Western Hemisphere from geostationary orbit, a full Earth disk image every 15 minutes, Cloud and Moisture Imagery as the key requirement, data latency no longer than the refresh time, a 120 Mbps raw data downlink and a 15-year fuel requirement. Budget, schedule and lifetime are game estimates sized for one large satellite.
